newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Drama seen continuing on Korean peninsula in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Drama seen continuing on Korean peninsula in 1997.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam begins his final year in office this week with his reform policies in tatters, and analysts expect him to take bold steps to regain his credibility.
They said Kim, with his political gambler's instincts, would almost certainly make dramatic efforts to win back support in the run-up to presidential elections in December.
Kim is constitutionally barred from seeking another term, but he has pressing reasons to ensure the victory of a hand-picked successor.
"I'm sure 1997 will be a tumultuous year for Korea," a Western diplomat said. "The danger is that Kim could put his personal interest before national interest."

Less than two months into the year, South Korea has been rocked by weeks of nationwide wildcat strikes, a loan scandal that landed a cabinet minister and close Kim associates behind bars and the defection of North Korea's top ideologue.

North of the border, meanwhile, two other top Pyongyang leaders quit the scene -- premier Kang Song-san was replaced, apparently for health reasons, and then on Saturday came news that powerful defence minister Choe Kwang had died.

The evident growing instability in the North promised to be a constant wild card in Seoul's political game, the diplomat said. "North Korea is lurking in every corner and could complicate things in the South."

"The opposition will try to make use of the ruling camp's blunders and the loan scandal to increase its chance of winning the presidential election," political science professor Cho Chang-hyun of Hanyang University said.
"The question is whether the issues will remain alive until the election," he said. "President Kim could well engineer a compelling new situation that would drown out all other issues."
In the past week, prosecutors have indicted 10 people, including three prominent Kim aides, on bribery and embezzlement charges, and have questioned the president's son over the loan scandal.

The prosecution cleared the son of any wrongdoing over the case on Saturday, however, and indicated that it had no plans to widen its investigation into loans of $5.8 billion that Hanbo Steel Co racked up before it became insolvent on January 23.
Opposition parties have demanded a new probe, saying state prosecutors had failed to uncover the "real big hands" in a scandal which has eaten into Kim's political credibility.

Kim, who took office on February 25, 1993, launched a high-profile anti-corruption drive yet a recent survey by the monthly magazine WIN showed that about 73 percent of those polled believed the president's reforms had failed.

The president's reformist image had also been tarnished by a controversial labour law, rammed through parliament in a dawn session while opposition deputies slept, a hawkish stance against North Korea, and a crackdown on student protests.

Kim's popularity, which topped 90 percent as he began his anti-graft campaign in 1993, is now hovering around 10 percent. The WIN survey showed 70 percent thought Kim himself should be investigated over the loan scandal if necessary.

Cho of Hanyang University said Kim, who put former presidents Chun Doo Hwan and Roh Tae-woo on trial for corruption, would try to install a protege in the presidential Blue House to protect him after he steps down.

In the past the incumbent president's support has been vital in the choice of a ruling party candidate, and analysts say Kim can be expected to delay as long as possible holding a party convention to pick the candidate to avoid becoming a lame duck.

Yeom Jaeho, a political science professor at Korea University, said the loan scandal had silenced fierce public criticisms raging over the controversial labour law only a month ago. Now news of the defection of high North Korean official Hwang Jang-yop had pushed the Hanbo case off the front pages.
Hwang, who sought asylum at South Korea's Beijing mission on February 12, is awaiting Chinese clearance to leave for Seoul.
"President Kim can be expected to pull something off to bring about a new phase," Yeom said.
Political commentators said North Korea, suffering from grave food shortages and economic hardship, might try and make a breakthrough in foreign relations and this could give Kim an opportunity.
Last year, Pyongyang's sabre-rattling unwittingly helped Kim score a thumping victory in parliamentary elections by pushing conservative voters to seek stability and rally behind him.
Gun-toting North Korean soldiers marched into the supposedly demilitarised border village of Panmunjom three times just days before the elections.
"North Koreans were the biggest contributor to our campaign," an official of Kim's party said at the time.
